ready1_open_rewrite.title: SciVerse open question
ready1_open_rewrite.rewritten_question_text: Glucose in solution often exists in a cyclic structure; ring formation is formed by the mutual reaction of the carbonyl group in the sugar molecule with the hydroxyl group on the penultimate carbon atom to form a hemiacetal or hemiketal. The configuration in which the hydroxyl group of $C_{1}$ is written below the ring plane is called $\alpha$-D-glucose.

method.method_draft: First describe the image as a cyclic D-glucose Haworth structure and identify the anomeric carbon C1 as the carbon next to the ring oxygen on the right. Read the substituents there: the hydroxyl on C1 is drawn below the ring plane. Combine this with the text’s criterion asking for the name of the configuration when the C1 hydroxyl is below the ring plane. Apply the alpha/beta convention for D-glucose and output the symbol alpha, i.e. α.

method.answer_match_reason: Predicted answer "α" is the same as the standard answer "\alpha".

answer_match_part_results.reason: They are identical representations of the Greek letter alpha.

planner_metadata.distinctiveness_rationale: This is the direct Haworth-projection classification route: it uses the attached ring drawing to locate the anomeric hydroxyl and then applies the alpha/beta naming convention. For this problem there is essentially only one honest solution route.
planner_metadata.image_role: Inspect the attached Haworth projection: the six-membered glucose ring has the ring oxygen at the upper right, the CH2OH group on C5 drawn above the ring, and at the rightmost anomeric carbon C1 the H is drawn above while the OH is drawn downward/below the ring plane.
planner_metadata.text_role: Read the Chinese prompt, which defines cyclic glucose formation and asks for the designation of the D-glucose configuration when the C1 hydroxyl is written below the ring plane.
planner_metadata.knowledge_role: For D-glucose in a Haworth projection, the anomer with the C1 hydroxyl below the ring plane, equivalently trans to the upward CH2OH group, is named alpha-D-glucose; if it were above it would be beta.
